item.title: Sean Winter Wins Poker Masters Finale As Adrian Mateos Clinches Purple Jacket
item.dc:creator: Card Player News Team
item.description:
Sean Winter won the $51,000 Poker Masters finale for $620,000, while Adrian Mateos held on to claim the 2026 purple jacket.

The post Sean Winter Wins Poker Masters Finale As Adrian Mateos Clinches Purple Jacket appeared first on Card Player.
item.content:encoded:
Sean Winter closed out the 2026 Poker Masters in style, taking down the $51,000 buy-in no-limit hold’em finale at the PokerGO Studio in Las Vegas for $620,000. The last event of the series also settled the race for the purple jacket, which went to Spanish star Adrian Mateos.

Winter topped a 31-entry field that built a prize pool of $1,550,000, with only the top five finishers paid. He defeated Sam Laskowitz heads-up to collect his second PokerGO Tour title of the year. Laskowitz earned $387,500 as the runner-up, which PGT reported as the best live tournament score of his career.

Winter came into the final day third in chips with seven players left. He told PokerNews that stepping away from the schedule for one tournament helped him find his form: “I wasn’t executing how I wanted to, and so I took an event off, the 15K, to just reset, and I think it worked out.”

The result moves Winter to 2,223 points on the 2026 PGT leaderboard, making him the first player to pass 2,000 points this season. He now has 17 cashes in PGT-qualifying events this year worth $4,391,694, and he is the clear frontrunner for PGT Player of the Year.

Mateos Holds Off Ausmus For The Purple Jacket

Mateos failed to cash in any of the last three events, which kept the leaderboard race alive until the very end. Jeremy Ausmus, who won event no. 7 earlier in the series, reached the final table needing at least a second-place finish to overtake him.

That chance slipped away in fourth place. Ausmus got his last chips in with pocket fives against Winter’s ace-king of diamonds, and an ace on the turn followed by another on the river ended his run with $170,500.

Mateos finished the series on 451 points from three cashes. Those were his win in event no. 5 for $229,500, a runner-up finish in event no. 2 and fourth place in event no. 7, for $467,700 in total. He also finished on the money bubble five times in ten events. Along with the purple jacket, he receives a $25,000 PGT Passport.

“I had a big lead all the way, but in the last three events I wasn’t able to cash, so the sweat was real,” Mateos told PokerNews.

Nicholas Palma ended the series second on 407 points, while event no. 9 champion Nicholas Seward took third on 397 points.

How The Final Table Played Out

Dan Smith was the first of the final seven to go. He moved all in with ace-eight over an open from Chris Brewer and could not catch up against the ace-queen of Marius Gierse. Brewer, who had earlier doubled with pocket aces against Smith’s ace-king, then busted on the bubble in sixth when his ace-jack ran into the pocket aces of Ausmus.

Gierse was the first player to cash, falling in fifth for $124,000 when his ten-nine could not beat the pocket queens of Laskowitz on a ten-seven-six flop. After Ausmus departed in fourth, Igor Yaroshevskyy shoved with queen-jack and was called by Winter’s king-ten, which held to send the Ukrainian home in third with $248,000.

Winter began heads-up with close to a three-to-one chip lead. Laskowitz briefly pulled even, but Winter rebuilt his advantage, and the tournament ended when his two pair held against the top pair of Laskowitz.

item.title: Poker Strategy With Alex Fitzgerald: The Pros Bluff Less Than You Think
item.dc:creator: Alex Fitzgerald
item.description:

The post Poker Strategy With Alex Fitzgerald: The Pros Bluff Less Than You Think appeared first on Card Player.
item.content:encoded:
In today’s strategy guide we are going to talk about some concepts that amateurs get completely wrong about professionals.

You Do Not Usually Need A Great Four-Bet Bluff Strategy

There is no need to develop a great four-bet bluff strategy 98% of the time. The vast majority of your opponents are simply not capable of three-bet bluffing enough.

I have been doing this job for 20 years. I have worked with thousands of clients from over 60 different countries. Most of my life is telling people to three-bet more, fold more, and bet more.

Yet, most people choose to be passive. And the place they choose to be passive the most is preflop.

They do not want to three-bet a decent hand, get four-bet off their hand, and then sit there frustrated wondering whether they would have hit the flop. So, they usually cold call too much.

I recently final-tabled a $1 million guaranteed tournament online, and that was a good example of when someone needs to three-bet more to get a big stack. My three-bet percentage in that tournament was around 14% or 15%.

If I saw one of my students on a similar run with a three-bet percentage of 11% to 13%, I would be really happy with that.

Unfortunately, the average person three-bets only around 6% to 7% of their hands. What does this mean for you?

A lot of people spend time studying how to four-bet bluff against someone who is three-betting too much, not realizing that player often does not exist in their games.

Even if somebody is three-betting you 14% of the time, that is still a pretty solid range. Most of the time, it will be hands that have decent equity post-flop, like K-9 suited or pocket eights. You do not need to overextend yourself against that range.

If you are out of position, open a slightly tighter range to deal with it. That is the maturity you need to develop.

You don’t need to four-bet bluff, because no one is three-bet bluffing you enough.

— Alexander Fitzgerald (@pokerheadrush) August 22, 2026

Almost No One Is Four-Bet Bluffing You

A lot of people see four-bet bluffs on TV and think everyone must be doing that. But the truth is that the vast majority of people almost never four-bet bluff.

They might know they are supposed to do it occasionally, but they would much rather call and take a flop.

If you three-bet a hand like jacks and someone four-bets you, ask yourself an honest question: Does my opponent even do this with tens, nines, or eights?

Sometimes you can make some disgustingly big laydowns simply because your opponent is that uncreative. But you have to give yourself the opportunity to make those folds.

Do not assume someone is making a high-level play just because you have seen high-level players do it on a stream.

There Are Not Nearly As Many Pros As You Think

The vast majority of poker players do not beat the rake. Of the maybe one person out of 10, or one person out of 20, who does beat the rake, the vast majority do not make a significant amount of money.

Of the players who do make a significant amount of money, the vast majority will not last more than three years.

So, if you are worried about being out of your element, understand that pretty much everybody else is trying to figure it out too. There is no reason to be intimidated.

A lot of guys try to act tough at the table, but you should not automatically believe them. Many of them are just as uncertain as everyone else.

Pros Bluff A Lot Less Than Amateurs Believe

Amateurs often believe the entire game is about bluffing. After all, that is the skill edge, right?

Well, in many games, it is not.

If you are playing in a game where everybody is calling way too much, your responsibility is to get the maximum amount of money by making thin value bets.

The skill edge might be value betting top pair third kicker for three streets and getting someone’s entire stack. That is not easy. And in that game, that is the skill edge.

It is not always about bluffing. There are simply fewer bluffing spots in that kind of game.

Obviously, there are tighter games where more bluffing spots are available. But that is not always what the game gives you.

You cannot force the way you want to play onto a game where it does not naturally fit.

Learn how to play A-K when it misses the flop!

Alexander Fitzgerald is a professional poker player and bestselling author who lives in Denver, Colorado. He is a WPT and EPT final tablist and has earned both WCOOP and SCOOP titles. He enjoys blasting bums away in online tournaments while he listens to death metal. Free training packages are provided to newsletter subscribers who sign up at PokerHeadRush.com.

item.content:encoded:
BCPoker is getting into the Halloween spirit with a new series featuring more than $50,000 in prizes, daily promotions, and the launch of the online poker room’s first-ever Mystery Bounty tournament.

The BCPoker Halloween Series runs from Oct. 24 through Nov. 5, with tournament buy-ins starting from freerolls. The schedule is headlined by the $20,000 Apex Halloween on Oct. 31, while a $1.5K Halloween Mystery Bounty will run daily from Oct. 30 through Nov. 5.

$20K Apex Halloween Headlines Tournament Schedule

The series opens with a pair of $300 Halloween Freerolls, with the first taking place Oct. 24 and the second returning on Halloween.

Players can also compete in the $1K Halloween Bounty each day from Oct. 25 through 29. The first seven players to score a knockout in each tournament will receive a $7 MTT ticket.

The biggest tournament of the series arrives Oct. 31, when the $20K Apex Halloween takes center stage.

BCPoker will also introduce its first Mystery Bounty tournament during the series. Beginning Oct. 30, the $1.5K Halloween Mystery Bounty will run daily at 18:00 UTC through Nov. 5, with an $11 buy-in.

Mystery Bounty tournaments add an element of surprise to every knockout, as players reveal a hidden cash bounty for each opponent they eliminate. Players won’t know the value of the bounty until it is claimed, meaning any knockout could produce a significant prize.

Daily Promotions Add More Ways To Win

The Halloween action extends beyond the tournament lobby with several promotions running throughout the series.

The Halloween Limited Edition Lucky Spin runs from Oct. 23 through Nov. 5, offering up to $1,000 in cash prizes along with Halloween tickets ranging from $2 to $50. Players can earn two spins per day by completing two NLHE cash game missions: playing 50 hands and winning 12 hands at their mission stakes. After five total spins, players can also earn a bonus Halloween ticket.

The $1,800 MTT KO Ranking runs Oct. 24 through Nov. 5, rewarding players based on their total knockouts in qualifying KO tournaments. Daily KO rewards of up to $5 are also available.

Meanwhile, the Boosted NLHE Leaderboard runs through Nov. 3, with $1,000 awarded every day to 100 winners based on their NLHE cash game play.

Players can access the Halloween Series through BCPoker’s web, desktop, mobile, or Telegram Mini App platforms. After logging in, players can open the tournament lobby and filter for the Halloween Series events.

About BCPoker

BCPoker maintains 1:1 proof of reserves, with player funds fully backed and stored separately from corporate assets. The platform also uses a decentralized random number generator, with BCPoker describing its games as certified provably fair.

The rising online poker site launched in 2025 as part of the BC.Game ecosystem, offering players a streamlined crypto-friendly poker experience with fast funding and global access. Game formats include hold’em, Omaha, and short deck.

The platform emphasizes player-focused design, strong security standards, and smooth gameplay. With up to 50% rakeback through the VIP program and crypto-friendly withdrawals, BCPoker makes a strong case for value hunters.

The post ACR Poker $500K Mystery PKO Gives Turbo Tuesday An Early Start appeared first on Card Player.
item.content:encoded:
Turbo Tuesday officially launches at ACR Poker on Oct. 27, but one of its main weekly tournaments is already underway. The first Day 1 flight of the new $500,000 guaranteed Mystery PKO started Wednesday, Oct. 21, giving players nearly a full week of starting-flight action before the opening Day 2.

The buy-in is $630, the top mystery bounty is $50,000, and the structure has an interesting feature for anyone planning to play more than one flight: qualifying stacks can be combined. Once the field reaches Day 2, the Mystery PKO format adds another decision to the mix, with every knockout potentially increasing the winner’s own bounty.

Sixteen Flights And A Chance To Combine Stacks

This isn’t a tournament with just one starting time. Each weekly edition has 16 Day 1 flights spread from Wednesday through Tuesday. Players can enter multiple flights, and any stacks they qualify with are combined when they move on to Day 2.

That changes the appeal of the starting schedule. Securing a Day 2 stack in one flight doesn’t necessarily mean being finished with the opening stage. A player who qualifies again can bring the combined chips into the next phase, rather than choosing between successful flights.

The first Day 2 begins Tuesday, Oct. 27, at 1:30 p.m. ET, with subsequent editions following the same weekly pattern. That’s also when the bounties come into play. The Day 1 flights are about getting through and building a stack; the knockout rewards start on Day 2, with play continuing until a champion is crowned.

Mystery Bounties Meet Progressive Bounties

The Mystery PKO format, exclusive to the Winning Poker Network, combines two kinds of knockout rewards. Each elimination during the bounty phase reveals a hidden mystery prize, but the player who scores the knockout doesn’t collect the entire prize immediately.

Instead, half of the mystery prize is paid out on the spot, while the other half is added to that player’s own visible bounty. Knock out an opponent and you can earn a payout while also becoming a more valuable target for everyone still in the tournament.

The progressive side works the same way. If the eliminated player has an accumulated progressive bounty, half of that amount is paid immediately to the player who knocked them out, while the remaining half is added to the winner’s bounty. In other words, both the mystery prize and an opponent’s existing progressive bounty can change the value attached to the player who gets the knockout.

What Happens If Someone Hits The $50,000 Prize?

The headline mystery prize makes the split easy to see. If a player reveals the $50,000 top mystery bounty, they receive $25,000 immediately. The other $25,000 goes onto their own visible bounty, where it becomes something their opponents can chase.

That’s an important distinction: the top mystery prize is worth $50,000, but it isn’t a $50,000 immediate payment. Part of that value follows the player onto the felt. The more bounties a player collects, the more attention their own growing bounty may attract.

It also gives the Day 2 field a different dynamic from a typical mystery bounty tournament. Knocking somebody out can bring an instant reward, but it can also raise the price on your own head for the hands that follow.

More Than 40 Turbo Tournaments Every Tuesday

The Mystery PKO is only one part of the broader Turbo Tuesday rollout. Starting Oct. 27, ACR Poker’s new weekly lineup includes more than 40 Turbo tournaments, with start times running from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. ET.

Every tournament in the Turbo lineup has late registration of two hours or less. That shorter registration window is a central part of the Tuesday schedule, giving players a recurring selection of faster-paced tournaments to choose from without having to commit to a lengthy late-registration period.

The timing also brings both sides of the launch together. Oct. 27 is the debut of the full Turbo Tuesday lineup and the first Day 2 of the $500K Mystery PKO. Players who have built stacks through the opening flights will move into the bounty stage as the wider Tuesday schedule gets underway.

About ACR Poker

ACR Poker has been a leader in online poker since 2001, serving players across the U.S., Latin America, and beyond.

The online poker site is renowned for its massive tournament guarantees and innovative formats. ACR Poker has a rewarding loyalty ecosystem which includes rakeback, reload bonuses, and leaderboard races.

item.title: Nicholas Seward Denies Daniel Negreanu At Poker Masters
item.dc:creator: Erik Fast
item.description:
Winning a PokerGO Tour title is a momentous achievement in any context. Nicholas Seward’s victory in Event No. 9 of the 2026 Poker Masters was made all the sweeter, though, given the caliber of competition he faced heads-up. Seward squared off against Poker Hall of Famer Daniel Negreanu at the close of the $25,000 buy-in […]

The post Nicholas Seward Denies Daniel Negreanu At Poker Masters appeared first on Card Player.
item.content:encoded:
Winning a PokerGO Tour title is a momentous achievement in any context. Nicholas Seward’s victory in Event No. 9 of the 2026 Poker Masters was made all the sweeter, though, given the caliber of competition he faced heads-up.

Seward squared off against Poker Hall of Famer Daniel Negreanu at the close of the $25,000 buy-in no-limit hold’em tournament, and managed to defeat the eight-time World Series of Poker bracelet winner to lock up the trophy and $412,500 in prize money.

This was the third-largest payday yet for the Washington, D.C. native. He now has more than $5.4 million in lifetime cashes, with his top score being the $516,135 that came with his first bracelet in the 2024 WSOP $3,000 six-max event. His next-biggest windfall was the $418,700 that came with his victory in this year’s World Poker Tour Venetian main event.

This triumph also came with plenty of ranking points. The 420 Card Player Player of the Year points he secured for his second title and 13th final-table finish of 2026 moved him inside the top 50 in the overall POY standings presented by CoinPoker.

With four cashes at this festival, including this win and two other top-five showings, Seward (397 points) now sits in third place in the series-long standings. He now trails only Adrian Mateos (451 points) and Nicholas Palma (407 points) in the race for the purple jacket.

Negreanu Leads Into Final Day

The 50-entry field produced a prize pool of $1,250,000, with that sum split amongst the top eight finishers. They made the money late on day 1, with series standings leader Adrian Mateos being eliminated on the direct bubble for the fifth time this series. The Spanish superstar has also won an event, finished as the runner-up, and placed fourth, accumulating $467,700 across those results.

David Coleman, who secured the purple jacket in 2025, was knocked out in eighth place ($50,000) before the remaining contenders bagged up for the night.

The final day began with Negreanu leading the final seven, while Seward sat in second chip position to start. Three-time bracelet winner Jesse Lonis was the first to fall. Just a few hands into the session, he called off the last of his stack from the big blind with K♦Q♣ facing an effective shot of 25 big blinds from Seward, who held J♥9♥. The Q♦J♦5♣ flop kept Lonis ahead, but the J♣ turn left him drawing to a queen with one card to come. The 7♥ rolled off instead and Lonis hit the rail in seventh place ($50,000). The reigning POY now has nearly $35.1 million in career cashes to his name.

With that, Seward overtook the top spot in the chip counts. Negreanu fell even further back when his K-J suited lost to K-Q for Sean Perry, who doubled off a short stack and into the middle of the pack.

Wilson And Perry Are Bounced To The Rail, While Negreanu Bounces Back

Brandon Wilson was left on fumes after losing most of his stack with A-2 suited against the pocket jacks of Seward. He then put his final 1.33 big blinds in with Q-7. He faced two opponents, and Negreanu bet Seward out on the river to win the pot with top set of kings. Wilson earned $75,000 as the sixth-place finisher. This was his third cash of the series, and 23rd final-table finish of 2026. He remains in second place in the POY standings, with 7,807 total points and more than $7.6 million in to-date POY earnings, with $18.1 million for his career.

As five-handed play continued, Negreanu picked up another key pot with pocket kings. He held off the A-J of Seward in an impactful clash to move back into pole position at the final table.

Negreanu then expanded his lead further via a showdown with Perry. Negreanu opened for an 80,000 min-raise from under the gun with J♠J♣ and Perry defended his big blind with 8♣6♣. The flop came down 10♣7♣3♥ to give Perry a gutshot straight flush draw. He checked to Negreanu, who fired 90,000. Perry check-raised to 255,000 and Negreanu moved all-in. Perry called off his stack and the 10♥ appeared on the turn. That left him needing a nine or a club on the river. The 2♥ on the end was no help to Perry, though, and he was sent to the rail in fifth place ($100,000).

This was the first final table in over three years for the former high-stakes tournament regular, who now focuses on sports betting. His poker earnings grew to $7.1 million with this performance.

Another BIG CLASH between @RealKidPoker and @seanperrywins!

Stream the @PokerGOTour’s Poker Masters, presented by @official_glp, on https://t.co/l4l4onsRIp. https://t.co/MKjdgGTGzt

— PokerGO (@PokerGO) October 22, 2026

Wantman And Gheba Bow Out Ahead Of Heads-Up

World Poker Tour champion and bracelet winner Matthew Wantman was the clear short stack going into four-handed action. He managed one double-up through Negreanu to buy some breathing room to start, but then ran into top two pair for Seward to give up much of his gains.

Wantman made his final stand with A♦Q♠, committing all but 20,000 of his stack preflop. Negreanu came along with K♦10♦ and flopped top pair. The remaining chips went in after a Q♣ turn. The 6♠ river changed nothing, and Wantman was eliminated in fourth place ($125,000). His lifetime tournament haul surpassed $14 million thanks to this latest deep run.

Daniyal Gheba, a bracelet winner who’s cashed in five of the first nine events at this festival, added another $175,000 to his tally with a third-place showing in this event. His last few big blinds went in with K♦6♦ facing A♣Q♦ for Seward. Neither player connected with a nine-high runout, and Gheba headed to collect his second six-figure payout of the week. His 2026 Poker Masters earnings now sit at $424,850 with one event left to play. His 348 points are good for fifth in the festival rankings.

Seward Survives Back-And-Forth Battle

Heads-up play began with Negreanu holding 4,200,000 to Seward’s 3,305,000. That gap was expanded in the early going, with Negreanu turning pocket tens into a bluff to force Seward off of second pair with K-J after an ace hit the turn.

Seward battled his way back into the lead, only for Negreanu to win a hefty pot with the nut flush to pull away again.

Things evened out again when Seward flopped quad kings after raising from the big blind. Negreanu limp-called with 4-3 suited and made kings and threes right off the bat. He hung around to the river, but folded when Seward went for the home run with a river jam.

The next key pot pitted Seward’s A♠6♥ against Negreanu’s Q♠J♣.  Seward raised to 225,000 preflop from the button and Negreanu defended. The flop brought the A♣6♠3♣ to give Seward aces up. Negreanu check-called 150,000 and picked up a club draw on the 9♣ turn. He led out for 375,000 and Seward called. The 6♣ improved both players, giving Negreanu a flush and Seward sixes full of aces. Negreanu fired 525,000 and Seward moved all-in. Negreanu went into the tank, but eventually folded and preserved his remaining 1,900,000.

Shortly after that, Negreanu got all-in with K♥10♦, three-bet shoving for 21 big blinds over Seward’s button open. Seward called with K♦J♥ and held through a 9♠3♠3♣5♣7♣ runout to bring the tournament to a close.

It’s all over! Nick Seward gets his first PGT title and $412,500. https://t.co/KxA1tyVWJm

— PokerGO (@PokerGO) October 23, 2026

After adding this $262,500, Negreanu’s career earnings have grown to $60.36 million. That’s good for 10th on poker’s all-time money list. He remains Canada’s top tournament earner, but Daniel Dvoress ($59.96 million) is hot on his heels.

item.content:encoded:
Autumn in the Pacific Northwest signals crisp morning air, turning leaves, and the return of a regional staple: the annual Fall Poker Round Up at Wildhorse Resort & Casino in Pendleton, Oregon.

The 2026 edition will run from Nov. 5-15, with 11 standard tournaments and five super satellites. Each of those 16 offerings features added money, totaling $30,000 for the series. The headliner is the $6,000 in added cash for the festival’s $550 buy-in no-limit hold’em main event.

This series has something for everyone, with buy-ins for the standard events ranging from $220 to $550. There are also multiple games and formats to choose from, including no-limit hold’em, Omaha eight-or-better, Omaha eight-or-better/seven card stud eight-or-better mix, H.E.R.O.S., and a seniors event for players aged 50 and older. 

For those looking to earn a seat in the aforementioned $550 main event for less, there are $115 buy-in super satellites running throughout the series.

Take a closer look at the full schedule below (click to enlarge and to view structure sheets for each event):

Reigning World Champ Headlines Stars Who First Shined At Wildhorse

Several Wildhorse Casino winners from recent years have gone on to make a splash on poker’s biggest stage, including reigning world champion Lucas Jumalon.

At the 2026 Spring Poker Round Up, the Washingtonian won the opening event. He outlasted 389 entries in the $220 event for $16,170 and his first recorded live title. Just a few months later, the 22-year-old Spokane resident took down the 2026 World Series of Poker main event for $10 million and his first gold bracelet. 

That incredible run came just a year after John Wasnock’s own impressive one-two punch in Pendleton and Las Vegas. Wasnock won the Spring Poker Round Up main event in 2025, besting a field of 584 to earn $56,330. A few months later, he finished second in the WSOP main event, earning $6 million after losing the heads-up battle against Poker Hall of Famer Michael Mizrachi.

There have been other examples of players making a name for themselves at the Round Ups. In 2015, Oregon’s Angela Jordison went on a winning spree that saw her secure three titles in a three-day span.

The festival has had impressive numbers in recent years. The latest main event, the 2026 Spring Poker Round Up, attracted 653 entries to build a $315,175 prize pool. Michael Jutte came out on top, earning $38,941 for the win. That was the Clarkston, Washington resident’s second main event victory at the venue after taking down the 2018 fall version. He boasts another three Round Up titles as well. 

About Wildhorse Casino

Wildhorse Resort & Casino is a destination resort in Pendleton, Oregon, offering casino gaming, hotel accommodations, dining, entertainment, golf, and family recreation. Wildhorse hosts multiple Poker Round Up tournament series throughout the year, and has been doing so for over two decades.

For players interested in attending the 2026 Fall Poker Round Up, hotel reservations on property are available at wildhorseresort.com, via the Wildhorse App, or by phone at 800-654-9453.

There are also accommodations available at preferred partner hotels, which are listed on the website and Wildhorse App.

Jumalon / Wasnock photo credits: WSOP.

item.content:encoded:
The craziest high-stakes action at CoinPoker this week took place in this epic heads-up PLO battle between two of the greatest four-card experts ever seen: Jared Bleznick and Eelis Pärssinen.

Bleznick was one of the first known players to take on these epic heads-up challenges at CoinPoker and has played a big part in putting these railbird games on the map.

The two locked horns over 971 hands, which is an incredible amount of volume for a single heads-up match. This was at $500/$1,000, the highest PLO stakes you will see anywhere.

In the end, it was “Theblez” who prevailed and took down $669,000, about as comprehensive a win as you will see at these stakes. Streamer Bobby James documented the whole match and picked out these key hands from this epic session:

Biggest Pot Of The Week

It was inevitable that the biggest battle of the week would lead to the biggest pot of the week.

It is impossible to get away from AJ on a JJ666 board when you make it so hard for your opponent to have anything else. Unfortunately for Jared Bleznick, his opponent also had AJ, but with an additional ace to hold the second nuts:

Sickest No-Limit Hand Of The Week

Kayhan Mokri has been taking on all comers this month at both No Limit and PLO, as documented by Mo Nuwwarah earlier this week. He also had the biggest No Limit pot of the last seven days.

A very gutsy hero call from “Deeeerp” in a spot where he knew Kayhan Mokri was very polarized. He either had a nutted hand or nothing, and unfortunately for Deeeerp, this time he had trips:

High Stakes Nostalgia

Once again, we look back at some of the craziest moments in the world of High Stakes Poker from years gone by. Returning to the show of the same name, this gutsy bluff by Brad Booth against Phil Ivey was considered by many to be the greatest bluff ever televised at the time.

Also check out the stacks of cash Booth was sitting behind.

The Biggest Winners Of The Week

Amazingly, despite the frenetic action at the highest stakes, the nosebleed community essentially broke even this week, in the sense that the biggest winner of the last seven days was only up $200k. This breaks a recent trend of the biggest winner of every week being up seven figures.

The post Polymarket Takes New Angle In Prediction Market Vs. State Court Battles appeared first on Card Player.
item.content:encoded:
Up until this point, the court battles between prediction markets and various U.S. states have followed a pretty set blueprint. The states argue that the prediction markets are improperly offering sports betting without a license. The prediction markets argue that they’re under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), so the states have no authority to bar them from doing business.

Polymarket has decided to try a new tactic. In a court filing against Ohio, the prediction market hit the familiar CFTC-centric note. But it also claims that the state is violating the Commerce Clause, gambling law expert Daniel Wallach reported.

BREAKING: Polymarket challenges constitutionality of Ohio’s online sports betting regime under the Commerce Clause, claims it discriminates against interstate commerce by requiring an in-state physical presence and in-state servers for licensing—calls it “unlawful protectionism.” https://t.co/a5ElkCA2vb

— Daniel Wallach (@WALLACHLEGAL) October 20, 2026

Polymarket Says Ohio Is Violating The Commerce Clause

The Commerce Clause is a part of the Constitution, one which “gives Congress broad power to regulate interstate commerce and restricts states from impairing interstate commerce.”

Ohio’s regulatory framework requires sports betting operators to have a physical presence in Ohio, including in-state servers. Polymarket argues that those policies constitute discrimination against out-of-state businesses seeking to profit from lawful interstate commerce.

“These discriminatory, balkanizing measures violate the Constitution’s promise of open, interstate commerce,” Polymarket said in its lawsuit. “And, under settled precedent, they are unlawful.”

Polymarket’s lawsuit comes in response to Ohio’s attempt to evict prediction market operators via cease-and-desist letters. The state sent letters to 10 prediction market operators, including Polymarket. The standard response from prediction markets in these instances has been to go on the offensive and sue the state, so Polymarket’s lawsuit hardly counts as a surprise.

The interesting part will be seeing whether the novel approach to the suit itself, invoking an alleged violation of the Commerce Clause, will bear any fruit. Thus far, the prediction markets have found the sledding fairly tough, with the states prevailing more often than not in court as things continue to build toward an eventual Supreme Court showdown.

Also In Prediction Market News

Betting On Court Cases Draws Ire To Prediction Markets

U.S. prediction markets are barred by law from offering contracts based on:

  • unlawful activity
  • assassination
  • terrorism
  • war
  • gaming
  • other similar activity contrary to the public interest.

That hasn’t stopped prediction markets from pushing the envelope when it comes to their offerings, and some recent listings on Polymarket have sparked backlash.

The harshest reaction followed Polymarket facilitating trades on whether any of the Cornell 7, fraternity members accused in a high-profile sexual assault case, would be charged with a felony sex crime. It’s important to note that this market was available on Polymarket’s international crypto-native exchange, which isn’t subject to the same laws as Polymarket US. Still, the public backlash was enough to convince Polymarket to remove the offering after more than $450,000 in trading volume.

Polymarket’s crypto exchange also offered markets centered around other high-profile cases, The Wall Street Journal reported. Legal experts say the situation raises myriad issues, including giving jurors motivation to bet on their own cases. Insider trading is another obvious concern.

A rep from Kalshi, Polymarket’s primary competitor, said the exchange wouldn’t consider offering similar markets.

Kalshi CEO Draws On Age-Old Black-Market Argument

Prediction market operators and sports betting operators may be born enemies, but that hasn’t stopped the prediction markets from parroting the same regulation-and-legalization arguments previously used by the online sportsbooks. Among the most tried-and-true: the argument that the betting will take place regardless, so disallowing it will just push it offshore.

Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour drew from that playbook in recent comments to CoinDesk:

“It’s not a choice of state versus federal market,” he said. “It’s a choice of whether prediction markets exist in the U.S. or whether they go offshore.”

The problem with that line of thinking is that it can be used to justify the existence of a lot of things that citizens and states don’t necessarily want. It also ignores the implicit social contract between governments and citizens, with the government having an obligation to institute policies that protect the populace.

Regardless of how hollow it rings, there’s real irony in the online sportsbooks’ biggest current opponent using their own argument to attempt to justify the existence of his competing product. If all Mansour wanted to do was rankle some sports betting executives, the best guess here is that he succeeded.

Gambling-Averse Utah Latest State To File Suit

The least gambling-friendly state in the country has filed another lawsuit against Kalshi. In some ways, that counts as the least surprising news of the week.

Along with Hawaii, Utah is one of two states that ban all forms of gambling. Kalshi is already appealing a court order allowing Utah to block prediction markets from operating there. Now, it is also facing a civil suit from the state seeking, in part, restitution of fees that Kalshi has raked in from Utah residents.

According to a local report, Utah is asking Kalshi to return between $30.6 million and $61.2 million in fees it may have profited at the expense of trades by Utahns.

“Frankly, they are engineered to do one thing and one thing alone, and that is empty your wallet,” said State Attorney General Derek Brown.

Utah argues in its filing that Kalshi’s contracts are “indistinguishable from the format of bets offered through any sportsbook.”

Billable hours continue to come out as the biggest winner in this ongoing fight.

item.content:encoded:
Keith Lehr soared to victory in the final $15,000 buy-in event of the 2026 Poker Masters. The 62-year-old Bossier City, Louisiana native defeated a field of 56 entries in the high-stakes affair to earn $277,200 and his second PokerGO Tour title. His first PGT win came in a pot-limit Omaha event back at the 2018 running of this same festival.

This result falls just outside of Lehr’s top-five scores. The two-time World Series of Poker bracelet winner’s career earnings now top $6.3 million. He now has 117 recorded cashes on the tournament circuit, with results dating as far back as 2002.

In addition to the title and the money, Lehr also secured 360 Card Player Player of the Year points and 222 PGT points for this latest strong showing. This was his second cash of the series, having previously placed sixth in event no. 5 for $42,500. With 265 total points, he’s moved to eighth in the race for the purple jacket.

Soverel, Seward Sent Packing Early

The top eight finishers made the money in this event, with $840,000 up for grabs. Event no. 7 champion Jeremy Ausmus (8th), Daniyal Gheba (7th), and event no. 2 winner Nicholas Palma (6th) were all eliminated late on day 1 after the bubble had already burst.

Event no. 4 champion Vitalijs Zavorotnijs held the chip lead heading into day 2, with Lehr sitting in fourth chip position to start. The action moved fast early, with two players falling inside the first hour of play. To start, 17-time PGT champion Sam Soverel made his final stand with K♦Q♥. He wound up all-in and at risk facing the A♥K♠ of Lehr. Neither player connected with a 10-high runout, and Soverel was eliminated in fifth place ($67,200). The four-time bracelet winner now boasts over $33.9 million in lifetime cashes.

Nicholas Seward soon followed. His run concluded in fourth place ($84,000) when he ran K♣10♥ into the A♠A♦ of Justin Vaysman in a battle of the blinds. Seward flopped top pair and a gutshot, but couldn’t improve on the turn or river. This was his third cash of the series. It grew the World Poker Tour champion and bracelet winner’s career earnings to more than $4.9 million.

It’s ACES for Justin Vaysman!

Watch the @PokerGOTour’s Poker Masters, presented by @official_glp, on https://t.co/l4l4onsjSR. https://t.co/zUF6a0Qc2e

— PokerGO (@PokerGO) October 21, 2026

Vaysman Bows Out

Fresh off his historic chip-and-a-chair comeback in event no. 6, Vaysman backed up his title run with a third-place finish in this tournament. The three-time bracelet winner parlayed his momentum from rallying from a quarter of a big blind just two days prior into another deep run.

Vaysman still held roughly 30 big blinds when his final hand arrived. He limped for 50,000 from the small blind with A♠6♦ and Zavorotnijs raised to 210,000 from the big blind with 10♥10♣. Vaysman shoved for 1,475,000 and received a quick call. He picked up an open-ended straight draw by the turn with 9♦8♣4♦7♠, but a blank J♦ on the end sent Vaysman packing with $117,600.

This score pushed Vaysman’s lifetime haul past the $2.1 million mark. The result marked his third final-table appearance of the festival, following the aforementioned results and a sixth-place finish in event no. 1. These deep runs have pushed him to fifth place on the series leaderboard with 325 points and $348,600 in earnings.

River Boat

Heads-up play began with 5,445,000 for Zavorotnijs and 2,995,000 for Lehr. The tables soon turned, though, with pocket kings holding against pocket fours to see Lehr double into the lead.

The next key clash began with Zavorotnijs opening to 170,000 on the button with A♠J♣. Lehr three-bet to 400,000 out of the big blind with K♣Q♠ and Zavorotnijs called. The flop came down Q♣10♠5♠ and Lehr fired 400,000. Zavorotnijs called and the K♠ rolled off on the turn, prompting an 800,000 bet from Lehr. Zavorotnijs moved all-in for 2,220,000 with the nut straight and an ace-high flush redraw and Lehr quickly called with top two pair. The Q♥ on the end improved Lehr to a full house to secure the pot and the title in dramatic fashion. Zavorotnijs settled for $176,400 as the runner-up.

WOW… what a way to win it! Keith Lehr takes the title in Event #8! https://t.co/TBTzFBwiKQ

— PokerGO (@PokerGO) October 21, 2026

Zavorotnijs moved to third place in the series-long standings, having accrued 365 points and $400,400 in total earnings. He now trails only Adrian Mateos (451 points) and Palma (407 points).

Final Table Results

Place Player Payout POY Points PGT Points
1 Keith Lehr $277,200 360 222
2 Vitalijs Zavorotnijs $176,400 300 141
3 Justin Vaysman $117,600 240 94
4 Nicholas Seward $84,000 180 67

6 Nicholas Palma $50,400 120 40

item.title: Poker Pro Bryn Kenney Sues GGPoker
item.dc:creator: Sean Chaffin

The post Poker Pro Bryn Kenney Sues GGPoker appeared first on Card Player.
item.content:encoded:
Poker pro Bryn Kenney has filed a lawsuit against GGPoker parent company NSUS Group. In the suit, Kenney claims the company cut his affiliate commissions by millions of dollars. He also alleges GGPoker backed out of a deal that would have given him a 5% ownership stake.

Kenney, one of poker’s all-time leading money winners, said GGPoker CEO Mansoo “Michael” Kim agreed in 2018 to give him recurring affiliate payments and an equity stake in the online poker brand. He further alleges the company concealed security flaws and knew players were cheating.

The lawsuit claims Kim later blamed Kenney for cheating taking place on the site. Kenney claims he helped build the platform’s high-roller scene.

He argues that the company recruited him to help grow the business when it was still a small operation. In the suit, he claims he recruited thousands of players and agents from 2018 to 2025 with the promise of the payments, the ownership stake, and becoming an ambassador for the platform.

Millions Of Dollars Unpaid

Kenney alleges breach of contract, fraudulent inducement, and other claims, and is seeking compensatory and punitive damages, along with a court-ordered accounting of company records.

“In the world of poker, deceit, misdirection, and misstatement are fair game,” the lawsuit says. “In the world of commerce, they are illegal.”

The lawsuit was originally filed in Clark County District Court in July but was transferred to U.S. District Court in August, according to the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

Kenney says the original affiliate agreement brought in about $5 million in 2019. However, the lawsuit alleges GG began removing players from his tracking system, limiting his earnings potential from players he recruited.

The suit alleges the company also began charging unauthorized fees and contacting sub-agents directly, further limiting his affiliate earnings. All this led to a drop in Kenney’s commissions to about $3 million by 2025.

The legal action alleges Kenney was never given the 5% stake in the company.

NSUS later went on to acquire the World Series of Poker in 2024 for $500 million, allegedly depriving him of a stake in that series as well. Kenney says his work for the company helped in the purchasing process.

He alleges Kim reneged on agreements that cost him millions of dollars.

The lawsuit says the CEO “made deliberate misrepresentations to plaintiff Bryn Kenney to induce Mr. Kenney to stake his reputation, personal finances, and years of labor to transform GGPoker from a failing, distrusted platform into the most recognized online poker room in the world. Having obtained the benefit of Mr. Kenney’s extraordinary contributions, defendants then methodically dishonored every material promise they made to him.”

Cheating Allegations

Beyond the financial implications, the lawsuit lays out assertions regarding cheating on the GG platform. Kenney claims Kim assured him security and anti-cheating teams were in place when he agreed to work for the company.

Kim allegedly knew of considerable cheating concerns but didn’t act to correct that, according to the lawsuit. Kenney further alleges Kim said the cheating came from players the high-stakes pro recruited.

Kenney said he guaranteed bankrolls for players and paid one player $1 million after Kim failed to pay out $6 million to players.

Along with the cheating allegations, Kenney says the company recruited American players and facilitated the use of the platform. If true, this would be in violation of U.S. regulations, where online gaming is legal on a state-by-state basis.

NSUS and Kim haven’t commented on the case. But they made a motion to dismiss the lawsuit on Sept. 23. A hearing is now scheduled for Nov. 12.

In the past, Kenney has faced cheating allegations. In 2022, Martin Zamani, a member of his player stable, said Kenney’s group had engaged in ghosting, used RTA (real-time assistance), and multi-accounted.

Zamani further alleged Kenney forced him to visit a shaman, who wanted to use frog poison on his open wound. Kenney denied all these allegations.

In September 2020, GGPoker banned 40 online poker accounts over suspected cheating, issued another 40 warnings, and confiscated nearly $1.2 million, which was returned to victims. The company also revealed a “superuser” incident in 2023 and confiscated $29,795 in unfair winnings.

The post Poker Pro Bryn Kenney Sues GGPoker appeared first on Card Player.
